docs.t: Judge Terence C. Kern (N.D. Okla.) — Pretrial conference
docs.x: Judge Terence C. Kern, N.D. Okla.. Pretrial conference: Be ready to argue exhibit objections, pending dispositive motions, and pending motions in limine; the court aims to end the conference with the case ready for trial. Also raise anything likely to cause sidebars or long argument at trial. Counsel must meet before the conference to review all proposed exhibits; claims at trial of never having seen a listed exhibit are disfavored.

docs.t: Judge Terence C. Kern (N.D. Okla.) — Motions in limine and Daubert
docs.x: Judge Terence C. Kern, N.D. Okla.. Motions in limine and Daubert: Strongly encouraged for complicated evidentiary issues; file by the scheduling-order deadline for decision at the pretrial conference. Untimely motions are not considered absent manifest injustice. Raise objections to scientific and expert testimony by timely motion in limine, and Daubert issues by Daubert motion under the scheduling order.

docs.t: Judge Terence C. Kern (N.D. Okla.) — Daily copy (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terence C. Kern, N.D. Okla.. Daily copy (trap): Daily transcripts are not allowed without prior approval, only in exceptional circumstances, on a motion heard at the pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Terence C. Kern (N.D. Okla.) — Voir dire
docs.x: Judge Terence C. Kern, N.D. Okla.. Voir dire: Attorney voir dire is allowed with time limits, 10–15 minutes per side unless more is approved before trial. Be ready to discuss voir dire areas and requested court questions at the pretrial conference. No previewing evidence or law, statements disguised as questions, hypotheticals, burden-of-proof explanations, or seeking promises from jurors.

docs.t: Judge Terence C. Kern (N.D. Okla.) — Exhibit and juror notebooks
docs.x: Judge Terence C. Kern, N.D. Okla.. Exhibit and juror notebooks: Prepare separate exhibit notebooks for the witness stand, opposing counsel, the court, and the law clerk; in voluminous cases, tailor notebooks to each witness or witness group. Try to agree on a joint exhibit set, with objected exhibits in separate plaintiff’s or defendant’s sets. Juror notebooks are rarely used; raise them at the pretrial conference and confer on contents before trial. Learn the Video Evidence Presentation System before trial (training through the Clerk’s office).

docs.t: Judge Terence C. Kern (N.D. Okla.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Terence C. Kern, N.D. Okla.. Trial: Juror note-taking is permitted; in 1–3 day trials the court gives no note-taking instruction unless asked. Closing argument follows the final instructions unless the court says otherwise.

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Motions in limine (trap): Motions in limine and motions for pretrial Rule 104 evidentiary hearings are due no later than 28 days before trial; oppositions 14 days after the motion is filed. Replies are ordinarily not required but may be filed within 3 days after the opposition. Notify chambers immediately of any pretrial motion requiring an evidentiary hearing. Motions in limine on deposition objections follow a separate 7-day deadline (see deposition designations). Objections to designated interrogatory answers and requests for admission are also raised by motion in limine on the 28-day schedule; the responses themselves must be designated by number in the pretrial conference order.

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Deposition designations (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Deposition designations (trap): Plaintiff designates by 28 days before trial; defendant counter-designates, designates its own, and objects by 21 days; plaintiff counter-designates and objects by 14 days. By 7 days before trial, file a color copy of the excerpts (plaintiff’s designations highlighted yellow, defendant’s green, objections in the margin), plus a motion in limine indexing every unresolved objection by page and line (NECivR 30.1(f)) and certifying the meet-and-confer required by NECivR 30.1(e). Form and foundation objections not made at the deposition are waived, and unnecessary objections should be withdrawn. After the rulings, the proponent edits the video (NECivR 32.1) or transcript designations and gives the other side time to review them. Deposition testimony of nonparty witnesses who testify live (in bench trials, any live witness) i

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Exhibits, witnesses, and experts (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Exhibits, witnesses, and experts (trap): Deliver two copies of trial exhibits to chambers 14 days before trial, in binders and in electronic format. NECivR 39.3 applies except as modified. At the pretrial conference with the magistrate judge (or as that judge orders), each party emails a Word exhibit list to both the magistrate judge’s and Judge Buescher’s chambers. Witness lists go in the pretrial conference order with addresses by city and state only; full names and complete addresses must be disclosed to the other parties by the pretrial conference. A witness who does not appear when scheduled is considered withdrawn. Deliver expert disclosures to chambers, in binders or digitally, 14 days before trial; any expert whose Rule 26 disclosure is not received by then (or earlier if requested) is considered withdrawn.

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Jury instructions: Meet and confer by 28 days before trial; by 21 days, file and email Word versions to chambers of a joint set of agreed instructions, a joint proposed verdict form, and, if needed, each party’s instructions on disputed issues. Instructions must be jury-ready and tailored to the case, based where possible on the Eighth Circuit Model Civil or Nebraska Civil Jury Instructions, with citations to authority. NECivR 51.1 applies except as modified. The court reads preliminary instructions after voir dire and before openings, gives the parties a preliminary set at the start of trial, holds one or more instruction conferences during trial, and gives final instructions before closing arguments.

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Trial briefs and interpreters
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Trial briefs and interpreters: Trial briefs are due no later than 7 days before trial and must comply with NECivR 39.2. A party needing an interpreter must retain one (a certified court interpreter if certification exists for the language, unless the court permits otherwise) and notify the courtroom deputy, Tracy McKibben (tracy_mckibben@ned.uscourts.gov, 402-661-7351), no later than 7 days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Trial schedule and jury
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Trial schedule and jury: Final pretrial conference in Courtroom 5 at 8:30 a.m. on the first day of trial; in jury cases, jury selection starts at 9 a.m. Trial hours are usually 9 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4:30 p.m., with 15-minute morning and afternoon breaks. Eight jurors are seated, and trial proceeds as long as at least six remain (NECivR 48.1). After a limited examination by the court, counsel generally get 20 minutes per party for voir dire. Jurors may take notes but may not ask or submit questions.

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Courtroom practice (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Courtroom practice (trap): Openings: up to 30 minutes per party. Closings: 30 minutes per party; plaintiff may reserve up to 15 minutes for true rebuttal that raises nothing new. The courtroom deputy keeps time and gives a 5-minute warning on request. No speaking objections; a foundation objection must state what foundation is lacking. Keep bench conferences to a minimum. Recross is not normally permitted, and cross and redirect are limited to the scope of the prior examination. Unless good cause exists, counsel must use the courtroom multimedia system and their own laptops to display exhibits; arrange training with the courtroom deputy beforehand. Exhibits may not be published to the jury without the court’s consent. Question from the podium, address witnesses and parties by surname, and use the table microphones; courtroom audio, including during br

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — After submission
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. After submission: Counsel must be available to return on short notice until the verdict and keep the courtroom deputy told where they can be reached. Jury questions are normally taken up on the record with counsel and the parties present.

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Settlement (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Settlement (trap): Counsel for all parties must notify the court immediately of a settlement, by email or phone to the assigned magistrate judge’s chambers or to Tracy McKibben during business hours. If settlement occurs within five days before trial, contact Tracy McKibben immediately by email or phone (402-661-7351).

docs.t: Judge Brian Craig Buescher (D. Neb.) — Bench trials and contact
docs.x: Judge Brian Craig Buescher, D. Neb.. Bench trials and contact: The non-jury order repeats the motion in limine, deposition, exhibit, witness, expert, trial brief, interpreter, opening, closing (including the 15-minute rebuttal), no-recross, and settlement rules, without the jury provisions. Email proposed orders to buescher@ned.uscourts.gov. The judge sits in Omaha, Courtroom 5.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Summary judgment: Judge Gerrard resolves summary judgment motions by the earlier of 60 days after the motion is ripe or 5 days before the pretrial conference. The court’s page states that all judges enforce NECivR 7.1 and 56.1; noncompliance will at least be noted in a written order, and harsher sanctions are possible.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Sentencing schedule (trap)
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Sentencing schedule (trap): The sentencing order sets dated deadlines for: versions of the offense to probation; financial information, restitution proposals, and evaluations; the initial PSR; written objections to probation; the revised PSR and addendum; then departure and variance motions, alternative-confinement proposals, and each party’s statement of position on unresolved objections. Before defense counsel submits PSR objections, the defendant must have read the initial PSR (or had it read by an interpreter) and had a chance to voice objections. Objections first raised in a statement of position are addressed at the judge’s discretion, and no sentencing factor first raised after the statement is filed will be considered.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Sentencing evidence and briefs
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Sentencing evidence and briefs: Evidence on a motion or objection comes by affidavit, letter, report, or other document attached to the statement of position, or by oral testimony requested in the statement, which must give the nature of the testimony, why documents won’t do, each witness, and the time needed for direct. The adverse party may make a responsive request within five working days. Brief any objection raising a substantial legal issue. Departure motions need a brief grounded in guideline departure theory; Booker variance motions need a brief explaining the different principle of law that justifies a non-guideline sentence.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Tentative findings (trap)
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Tentative findings (trap): The judge issues rulings and tentative findings and says whether oral testimony will be permitted. An oral objection at sentencing suffices only if no evidence and no new substantial legal issue will be offered. Otherwise, file a written objection no later than five business days before sentencing (if time does not permit, as soon as possible but no later than one business day before). If offering evidence, say why a hearing is needed, what evidence, and how long; brief any new substantial legal issue.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Criminal jury trial basics
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Criminal jury trial basics: Trial hours: 8:45 a.m. to noon and 1:15 to 4:30 p.m., with 15-minute morning and afternoon breaks. The court conducts a general voir dire, then each lawyer gets 20 minutes. Openings: 20 minutes per party. Closings: 30 minutes per party, with up to 10 minutes reserved for true rebuttal. Counsel may remain seated to question witnesses, should remain seated when digital audio is in use, and may not move about the courtroom during openings and closings when it is in use.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Jury instructions (trap)
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Jury instructions (trap): Submit requested instructions as the order setting trial directs, but no later than 1 business day before trial. Preliminary instructions are given after voir dire and before openings, with the proposed set provided to counsel before trial. Final instructions are given before closing arguments, with a “housekeeping” instruction after. An informal, off-the-record conference near the end of trial is followed by a formal on-the-record conference.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Jurors (trap)
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Jurors (trap): Be prepared to state whether you want alternates seated; if none is seated, be prepared to stipulate that 11 jurors may return a verdict whenever the 12th is excused. Jurors may take notes but may not ask questions.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Exhibits, objections, and examination
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Exhibits, objections, and examination: Pre-mark exhibits and list them on court-approved forms where practical; give received exhibits to the courtroom deputy, and turn in unoffered or unreceived listed exhibits at the close of trial. Before exhibits go to the jury, counsel confer in the deputy’s presence about which ones go. Provide the judge a copy of each exhibit. No speaking objections; a foundation objection must state what is lacking. Bench conferences should be infrequent and only for good cause. Recross is not normally permitted, and cross and redirect are limited to the scope of the prior examination.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Recording and courtroom
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Recording and courtroom: The judge uses either a court reporter or digital audio (counsel are told in advance); digital recordings are uploaded to CM/ECF after each day. Always speak into a microphone, including the presenter microphone when using the video presenter, or you will be interrupted. Courtroom audio, including during recesses, is broadcast to chambers. In Lincoln, for security, the defendant and defense counsel must use the table by the east wall, not the one by the jury box. Counsel must stay in the courthouse or be available on short notice until the verdict; jury questions are taken up on the record with the defendant present.

docs.t: Judge John Melvin Gerrard (D. Neb.) — Recusals and contact
docs.x: Judge John Melvin Gerrard, D. Neb.. Recusals and contact: The posted recusal list (last updated July 21, 2020) shows the City of Lincoln. Email proposed orders to gerrard@ned.uscourts.gov. The judge sits in Lincoln, Courtroom 3.

docs.t: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon (D. Neb.) — Brief length (trap)
docs.x: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon, D. Neb.. Brief length (trap): Except in extremely complicated cases (for example, patent and some securities cases), Judge Bataillon prefers briefs under 25 pages, not counting the section numbering contested and uncontested issues. Employment discrimination, social security, basic contract, and tort cases are generally not complicated, and most motions to dismiss or for summary judgment do not need more than 25 pages.

docs.t: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon (D. Neb.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon, D. Neb.. Summary judgment: Judge Bataillon resolves summary judgment motions by the earlier of 60 days after the motion is ripe or 5 days before the pretrial conference. The court’s page states that all judges enforce NECivR 7.1 and 56.1; noncompliance will at least be noted in a written order, and harsher sanctions are possible.

docs.t: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon (D. Neb.) — Sentencing schedule (trap)
docs.x: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon, D. Neb.. Before defense counsel submits PSR objections, the defendant must have read the initial PSR (or had it read by an interpreter) and had a chance to voice objections. Objections first raised in a statement of position are addressed at the judge’s discretion, and no sentencing factor first raised after the statement is filed will be considered.

docs.t: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon (D. Neb.) — Sentencing hearing length (trap)
docs.x: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon, D. Neb.. Sentencing hearing length (trap): One week before sentencing, counsel must notify the judge if the hearing is expected to last longer than one-half hour.

docs.t: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon (D. Neb.) — Sentencing evidence and briefs
docs.x: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon, D. Neb.. Sentencing evidence and briefs: Evidence on a motion or objection comes by affidavit, letter, report, or other document attached to the statement of position, or by oral testimony requested in the statement, which must give the nature of the testimony, why documents won’t do, each witness, and the time needed for direct. The adverse party may make a responsive request within five working days. Brief any objection raising a substantial legal issue. Departure motions need a brief grounded in guideline departure theory; Booker variance motions need a brief explaining the different principle of law that justifies a non-guideline sentence.

docs.t: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon (D. Neb.) — Contact
docs.x: Judge Joseph F. Bataillon, D. Neb.. Contact: Email proposed orders to bataillon@ned.uscourts.gov. The judge sits in Omaha, Courtroom 3.

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — Civil jury instructions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. Civil jury instructions (trap): Counsel must meet and confer, without the court, to build a complete joint set. At least two weeks before trial, file and email Word versions to chambers of a joint set of agreed instructions, a joint proposed verdict form, and, if necessary, each party’s instructions on disputed issues (see also the Final Progression Order and NECivR 51.1). Instructions must be jury-ready and tailored to the facts, not abstract propositions of law, based where possible on the Eighth Circuit Model Civil, Nebraska Civil, or other pattern instructions. The court holds an informal, off-the-record instruction conference in chambers during trial, then a formal on-the-record conference. Final substantive instructions are given after closing arguments (civil and criminal).

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — Preliminary instructions
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. Preliminary instructions: In jury trials the court reads a standard preliminary Instruction No. 1 after voir dire and before openings; counsel receive a copy 10 days before trial. In criminal cases, final instructions follow the Trial Order.

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — Trial hours and jury
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. Trial hours and jury: Jury trials usually run 9 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 4:30 p.m.; bench trials 9 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4:30 p.m., with 15-minute morning and afternoon breaks. Civil juries generally have eight jurors and no alternates (NECivR 48.1). Criminal trials seat 12 jurors and usually one alternate. After a limited examination by the court (NECivR 47.1(a) in civil cases), counsel generally get 20 minutes per party for voir dire. Jurors may take notes but may not ask or submit questions.

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — Openings and closings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. Openings and closings (trap): Openings: up to 30 minutes. Closings: 30 minutes per party. In jury trials, the plaintiff or government may reserve up to 10 minutes (one-third of its time) for rebuttal, never more than half the time actually used; in bench trials, closings are on request and the plaintiff may reserve up to 15 minutes. Rebuttal must be true rebuttal and raise nothing not addressed in the first argument (in criminal cases, or in the defendant’s closing). The courtroom deputy keeps time and gives a 5-minute warning on request.

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — Objections and examination (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. Objections and examination (trap): No speaking objections in jury trials; a foundation objection must state what foundation is lacking. Ask for a bench conference and allow the court reporter time to set up; keep them to a minimum. Recross is not permitted (in bench trials, not normally). Cross is limited to the scope of direct, and redirect to the scope of cross. Question from the podium unless directed otherwise, and refer to witnesses and parties by surname absent permission.

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — Exhibits and evidence presentation (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. Exhibits and evidence presentation (trap): Civil exhibits follow NECivR 39.3; criminal exhibits follow the Trial Order and must be numbered consecutively, with separate exhibits numbered separately and every page of a multi-page exhibit numbered. Do not use letters for exhibits or pages. Unless good cause exists, counsel must use the courtroom multimedia system, including the video presenter, and their own laptops to display exhibits; contact the courtroom deputy for training and test audio, video, and electronic presentations before trial. The deputy generally controls publishing to the jury on the judge’s instruction.

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — Courtroom logistics
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. Courtroom logistics: Plaintiff’s or the government’s counsel uses the tables nearest the jury box; defense counsel the tables farthest away. Pull the podium and table microphones about six inches in front of you; mute them for client conferences. Anything said in the courtroom, including during breaks, is broadcast to chambers.

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — After submission
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. After submission: Counsel must be available to return on short notice until the verdict and keep the courtroom deputy told where they can be reached. Jury questions are normally taken up on the record with counsel present.

docs.t: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr. (D. Neb.) — Cross-references and contact
docs.x: Judge Robert F. Rossiter Jr., D. Neb.. Cross-references and contact: Civil jury trials: trial briefs under NECivR 39.2, witnesses under NECivR 16.2(a)(2)(D), and depositions under NECivR 30.1 and 32.1. Bench-trial depositions follow the Final Progression Order; criminal depositions follow the Trial Order. Email proposed orders to rossiter@ned.uscourts.gov. The judge sits in Omaha, Courtroom 4.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Motions and briefing
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Motions and briefing: Leave to exceed the prescribed page length must be sought by motion. Label exhibits clearly. If memoranda reference deposition excerpts, the judge prefers having the full condensed transcript available. Hearings on civil motions are rare; put all arguments and authority in the memoranda supporting and opposing the motion.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Proposed orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Proposed orders (trap): File a proposed order as an attachment to every non-dispositive motion. Submit proposed orders, proposed jury instructions, and proposed findings and conclusions in PDF through CM/ECF.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Emergency motions
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Emergency motions: For TROs and select discovery motions, do not call chambers until the matter is assigned to Judge Dever; then tell the intake deputy clerk it needs immediate attention. Except in admiralty matters, the judge generally asks the movant to confer with opposing counsel to try to agree on temporary injunctive action pending the preliminary injunction hearing.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Protective orders and sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Protective orders and sealing (trap): Before submitting a proposed consent protective order, review Hall v. United Airlines, Inc., 296 F. Supp. 2d 652, 678–80 (E.D.N.C. 2003), and Local Civil Rule 79.2. The judge’s model language: before filing material designated confidential, confer with the producing party; if it wants sealing, file under L. Civ. R. 79.2 with notice to it, and within 10 days of that notice the producing party (not the filer) must move to seal with a supporting memorandum. If no timely motion is filed, the materials are deemed unsealed without further order.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Civil pretrial
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Civil pretrial: Pretrial is set after all dispositive motions are heard, and the pretrial conference usually comes about two weeks before trial; it will not automatically be continued if dispositive motions are still pending. Submit all expert material (CVs, reports, depositions, and objections to qualifications) to chambers before trial for the court’s gatekeeping function. The judge prefers a hearing near trial to rule on Pretrial Order objections; at trial, all exhibits are deemed admitted except those on which ruling was reserved. Parties may consent to a magistrate judge, including trial on a date certain.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Criminal terms (trap)
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Criminal terms (trap): Motions to continue (including by Probation) are due at least 5 business days before the session begins, absent exigent circumstances, with a proposed order; orders continuing arraignment must contain speedy-trial language from 18 U.S.C. § 3161(h). All attorneys, agents, and defendants must be seated at 9:00 a.m. on the first day of the term, when the docket is called; defendants to be arraigned must hear the half-hour “litany,” and a late defendant will be taken into custody. Arraignments and Rule 11 pleas are on day one, with sentencings and motions following. All juries for the term are picked the same day; express trial-order preferences to the courtroom deputy at least a week before the term.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Scheduling conflicts
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Scheduling conflicts: Send “conflict letters” to each judge whose docket is affected; staff will resolve the conflict. Federal prosecutors and defenders should try to hand off routine matters internally first.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Trial: Prepare a tabbed exhibit notebook for the judge and the law clerk; reduce large exhibits to 8 1/2" x 11" for the record. To use court-owned evidence-presentation equipment, contact the Clerk’s office one week before trial; equipment not owned by the court is not available to litigants. Question witnesses seated at counsel table unless discussing an exhibit at the stand. No argument in openings; the judge will stop it.

docs.t: Judge James C. Dever III (E.D.N.C.) — Courtroom conduct
docs.x: Judge James C. Dever III, E.D.N.C.. Courtroom conduct: Cell phones are prohibited in the courtroom. The judge is punctual and expects the same; gamesmanship, sandbagging, name-calling, or other unbecoming conduct will not be tolerated.

docs.t: Judge Louise W. Flanagan (E.D.N.C.) — Contacting the court (trap)
docs.x: Judge Louise W. Flanagan, E.D.N.C.. Contacting the court (trap): Do not contact chambers about calendar conflicts or case matters; direct them to the clerk’s New Bern office at (252) 638-8534. Resolve scheduling conflicts under the court’s Guidelines for Resolving Scheduling Conflicts, 85-PLR-3. Filings made outside business hours are not reviewed until the next business day at the earliest.

docs.t: Judge Louise W. Flanagan (E.D.N.C.) — Motions and briefing
docs.x: Judge Louise W. Flanagan, E.D.N.C.. Motions and briefing: Where practicable, cite previously or simultaneously filed exhibits with hyperlinks, preferably to the specific page; the judge encourages hyperlinking and “electronic briefs” for lengthy documents. Every motion requesting relief (except dispositive motions) must be accompanied by a proposed order, in PDF, filed as an attachment to the motion. A motion to amend a pleading must attach both the proposed amended pleading and a red-lined version showing the changes.

docs.t: Judge Louise W. Flanagan (E.D.N.C.) — Expedited relief (trap)
docs.x: Judge Louise W. Flanagan, E.D.N.C.. Expedited relief (trap): Do not call the case manager until the matter is assigned to Judge Flanagan. Once assigned, and before filing any motion needing expedited action, call the case manager at (252) 638-8534. Except in admiralty matters, the judge may ask the movant to confer with opposing counsel to agree on temporary action pending a hearing.

docs.t: Judge Louise W. Flanagan (E.D.N.C.) — Civil case management
docs.x: Judge Louise W. Flanagan, E.D.N.C.. Civil case management: In most civil cases the judge holds a brief (normally 20-minute) initial telephonic conference once the pleadings are framed, after a joint report and plan submitted as directed in the initial scheduling order. A comprehensive case management order follows. Deadlines may be extended for good cause, but the judge warns that excessive extensions undermine the case plan.

docs.t: Judge Louise W. Flanagan (E.D.N.C.) — Trial schedule and jury
docs.x: Judge Louise W. Flanagan, E.D.N.C.. Trial schedule and jury: Unless otherwise noticed, be present and available for conference at least 30 minutes before jury selection on day one. Court breaks about noon for an hour and usually recesses around 5:30 p.m., with one 10–15 minute break each morning and afternoon; be ready to take up issues during breaks. The judge conducts voir dire; parties may suggest additional questions by the deadline set in the case. The court uses the Arizona struck jury process, jurors may take notes, and the jury is instructed orally after closings and gets written instructions. A charge conference precedes closings.

docs.t: Judge Louise W. Flanagan (E.D.N.C.) — Trial conduct (trap)
docs.x: Judge Louise W. Flanagan, E.D.N.C.. Trial conduct (trap): Question witnesses seated at counsel table unless discussing an exhibit at the stand, and ask permission before approaching a witness the first time. Exhibits may be used in opening statements only by agreement of the parties. Stand and briefly state the ground for an objection, ordinarily without argument. Absent objection, permission to publish admitted evidence to the jury may be assumed. Contact the courtroom deputy at (252) 638-8534 well before trial for instruction on the courtroom technology and file formats; see 05-PLR-7 on wireless devices.

docs.t: Judge Louise W. Flanagan (E.D.N.C.) — Criminal sentencing and Rule 35
docs.x: Judge Louise W. Flanagan, E.D.N.C.. Criminal sentencing and Rule 35: Oral character testimony is ordinarily not allowed at sentencing. Statements, letters, and affidavits must be filed under seal and served on the government at least 7 days before sentencing; if more than five, index them with a brief description, the writer’s name, and relationship to the defendant. A Rule 35 motion must state the facts, any U.S. Attorney recommendation on the extent of departure, and confirm the government conferred with defense counsel in advance on whether there are compelling reasons it cannot be heard without the defendant. The defendant ordinarily need not attend.

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Motions and briefing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Motions and briefing (trap): Before filing any motion, confer with the other side and state in the motion your efforts to confer and the opposing party’s position (opposed, unopposed, or none). Leave to exceed page limits must be sought by motion. Record citations must give exhibit, page, and line; where practicable, hyperlink cited exhibits, preferably to the specific page. If memoranda reference deposition excerpts, file the entire transcript in original form; condensed transcripts are unacceptable. A motion to amend must attach the signed proposed amended pleading and a red-lined version. Civil motion hearings are rare; put all argument and authority in the briefs.

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Proposed orders: Every motion requesting relief (except dispositive motions and, in criminal cases, motions to continue, seal, and withdraw) must come with a proposed order. File proposed orders, jury instructions, and findings and conclusions in PDF through CM/ECF, and also email proposed orders in Word to Documents_Judge_Myers@nced.uscourts.gov (receipt only).

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Courtesy copies (trap): In civil cases, provide a courtesy copy of every filing of 100 or more pages, including attachments and exhibits, with the CM/ECF stamp, in a three-ring binder tabbed by docket entry and exhibit number. Mail or deliver to the Clerk, U.S. District Court, E.D.N.C., 2 Princess Street, Wilmington, NC 28401.

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Hearings, calendar changes, and emergencies
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Hearings, calendar changes, and emergencies: Hearings ordinarily start at 10:00 a.m. Calendar change requests must be made by motion stating the opposing party’s position; requests by email to chambers or the Clerk will not be entertained. For emergency motions (TROs, select discovery motions), do not call chambers until the case is assigned to Chief Judge Myers; then tell the intake deputy clerk or civil case manager it needs immediate attention. Except in admiralty, the judge generally asks the movant to try to agree with opposing counsel on temporary relief pending the preliminary injunction hearing.

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Civil pretrial
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Civil pretrial: Most pretrial matters go to the magistrate judge until the calendar is published, except in complex litigation; parties may consent to a magistrate judge, including trial on a date certain. Once pretrial and trial dates are set, a request to extend discovery or dispositive-motion deadlines must also request a matching continuance of the pretrial conference and trial. The pretrial conference is usually about two weeks before trial and is not automatically continued for pending dispositive motions. Submit expert (“opinion witness”) materials to chambers per the trial scheduling order; the court rules on Pretrial Order objections near trial, and other exhibits are deemed admitted.

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Criminal deadlines (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Criminal deadlines (trap): Most deadlines run from the first day of the term: motions to continue at least 3 business days before (otherwise heard in person at the hearing absent exigent circumstances, and non-sentencing continuances must satisfy 18 U.S.C. § 3161(h)); other non-emergency motions at least 5 business days before, or filed by 4:00 p.m. and heard in open court with all present. Proposed plea agreements go to the criminal case manager (angela_shoe@nced.uscourts.gov) at least 5 business days before the term. Check the penalty sheet (prison range, supervised release, maximum fine, revocation term), that an Information is not called an “Indictment,” and that multi-count pleas state cumulative penalties. Defendants must be in court by 10:00 a.m.; late defendants on bond will be taken into custody. Sentencing motions, memoranda, and character l

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Visual aids in opening and closing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Visual aids in opening and closing (trap): Under 22-JP-1-M (May 9, 2022), counsel may use visual aids showing admitted or stipulated exhibits. Any other demonstrative in opening, including charts, timelines, and summaries of admitted evidence, needs court approval after the other side can comment; depictions of approved jury instructions need no pre-approval.

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Trial: Criminal trials preempt civil trials. Jury selection starts at 10:00 a.m., all juries for a term are picked the same day (Arizona struck jury), and court then resumes at 9:30 a.m. daily. Jurors may take notes. No argument in openings. Each side chooses closing length, with equal time, and rebuttal may not exceed the closing. The charge conference and oral instructions come before closings; the jury gets written instructions. Pre-mark exhibits per L. Civ. R. 39.1(b), prepare two tabbed exhibit notebooks, and reduce large exhibits to 8 1/2" x 11". Question witnesses seated at counsel table unless discussing an exhibit at the stand; arrange a microphone in advance to work from the well. Email documents required by L. Civ. R. 39.1, 51.1, and 52.1 to the Documents_Judge_Myers address.

docs.t: Judge Richard E. Myers II (E.D.N.C.) — Special appearances and decorum
docs.x: Judge Richard E. Myers II, E.D.N.C.. Special appearances and decorum: If special-appearance rules (L. Civ. R. 83.1(e)(5), L. Crim. R. 57.1(e)(5)) appear violated, 22-JP-2-M is filed and counsel must show cause within 14 days why they should not be removed. The judge will not tolerate gamesmanship, sandbagging, or name-calling. In Wilmington high-attendance proceedings (22-JP-3-M), everyone needs photo ID, must be seated 15 minutes early, and may move only at recesses.

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Courtesy copies (trap): The filer must provide a courtesy copy of every document of 20 or more pages, including attachments and exhibits. Mail or deliver to the Raleigh Clerk’s Office, 310 New Bern Avenue, Room 574, Raleigh, NC 27601, to the attention of Lindsay Stouch (civil and miscellaneous), Linda Downing (criminal), or the Prisoner Section (habeas and prisoner cases).

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Filing and briefing
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Filing and briefing: Leave to exceed page limits must be sought by motion; review Local Civil Rule 7.2. Label all attachments and exhibits clearly.

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Civil trial setting (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Civil trial setting (trap): Under 02-JP-1-BO, in all civil cases (including habeas, admiralty, and miscellaneous civil proceedings) the court may set the case for trial 30 days after the dispositive-motion deadline, and scheduling orders are conformed to that rule.

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Civil trial witnesses (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Civil trial witnesses (trap): Video deposition testimony is prohibited in civil trials unless specifically allowed by order (May 5, 2023 order). Subpoena all witnesses at least 14 calendar days before the first day of the trial term in which the case is calendared.

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Criminal continuances and filings
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Criminal continuances and filings: To continue a criminal matter from a scheduled session, file a motion and a proposed order stating: “For good cause shown, [ ]’s Motion to Continue is hereby GRANTED and this matter is continued to the _ term of court.” The court may reset any scheduled matter at its discretion (08-JP-1-BO). Once a defendant has counsel, only counsel may file (other than a motion for new counsel). Pro se filings are docketed but not acted on unless re-filed by counsel, and pro se motions are terminated without order (11-JP-3-BO).

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Victim participation
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Victim participation: In criminal matters, the government must notify the court at least 10 days before any proceeding whether victim participation is anticipated; the notice may be filed ex parte and under seal for good cause (17-JP-1-BO).

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Section 4248 commitments
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Section 4248 commitments: Standing Order 11-SO-4 applies except that the government must move to appoint an examiner of its choosing on filing or within 10 days, the court then enters a preliminary order appointing the first examiner, and the respondent must move to appoint its examiner within 14 days of that appointment (12-JP-1-BO).

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Social Security appeals
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Social Security appeals: The U.S. Attorney need not appear for the United States at Social Security appeal hearings; representation may be delegated to agency counsel (16-JP-1-BO, vacating 15-JP-1-BO).

docs.t: Judge Terrence W. Boyle (E.D.N.C.) — Special appearances
docs.x: Judge Terrence W. Boyle, E.D.N.C.. Special appearances: If the special-appearance rules (L. Civ. R. 83.1(e)(5), L. Crim. R. 57.1(e)(5)) appear violated, 22-JP-1-BO is filed in the case and counsel must show cause within 14 days why they should not be removed.

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Requests to the court (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Requests to the court (trap): Ask for relief by written motion under the Local Rules; requests by letter or informal correspondence are disfavored and may be denied out of hand. Changes to deadlines or scheduling orders need a motion that describes specifically the efforts made to get the other side’s consent and whether it was obtained. Informal agreements among counsel to change court deadlines do not bind the court, and pending motions or settlement talks do not justify changing the schedule or delaying discovery. Counsel seeking non-dispositive procedural relief must consult the other side and state in the motion whether it is opposed.

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Chambers contact and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Chambers contact and proposed orders: Ex parte communication with the judge is prohibited; communicate with chambers in writing. Calls are limited to procedural or scheduling matters, such as getting, moving, or canceling a hearing, confirming receipt of a proposed order, or flagging an emergency filing, a filing affecting an imminent hearing, or a filing the court required by a set time. Chambers: 414-297-3071. Proposed orders go two ways: e-filed in PDF as an attachment to the motion or stipulation, and emailed in Word (not PDF) to LudwigPO@wied.uscourts.gov with the case name and number in the subject line. They are generally not needed for motions to dismiss, summary judgment, or other motions likely to get a written decision. No courtesy copies of briefs are required.

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Hearings and remote appearances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Hearings and remote appearances (trap): Most motions are decided without a hearing; request oral argument in your motion papers if you think it would help. The hearing notice says whether the hearing is in person, by phone, or by video. To appear remotely when the notice does not allow it, file a Civil L. R. 7(h) motion in advance explaining the need. For phone hearings, call 1-669-254-5252, Meeting ID 160 9600 2659 #, Passcode 243805, at least five minutes early; phone hearings generally are not used to take evidence. To reschedule a hearing, call chambers with all interested parties on the line; if you can’t get everyone on, file a motion. Hearings are digitally recorded and audio is usually posted to the docket. Ask by motion in advance if you think an in-person court reporter is needed.

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Emergency and expedited relief
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Emergency and expedited relief: Do not call to schedule an emergency hearing until you have filed a motion for the relief; then you may contact chambers to schedule. Non-dispositive matters needing expedited, but not emergency, relief use Civil L. R. 7(h).

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Scheduling conference and orders
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Scheduling conference and orders: Scheduling conferences are generally by phone. Hold the Rule 26(f) conference at least 21 days before and file the discovery-plan report no later than 7 days before, proposing dates for initial disclosures, amended pleadings, fact discovery, primary and rebuttal expert disclosures, expert discovery, dispositive motions, and class certification motions if applicable. Most cases should be ready for resolution within one year of filing; be ready to explain why a case needs more time. Under the form order, discovery requests must be served early enough that responses are due before the discovery cutoff, and expert disclosures are exchanged, not filed. The FLSA/Rule 23 form also sets deadlines for conditional certification, decertification, and class certification motions.

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Discovery disputes and protective orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Discovery disputes and protective orders (trap): The court expects most discovery issues to be resolved without it; if not, use the expedited non-dispositive motion procedure in Civil L. R. 7(h). The court will not enter a protective order without specific facts establishing good cause; a bare stipulation without a factual basis is not enough (Civil L. R. 26(e)).

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Summary judgment: Summary judgment motions must comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 56 and Civil L. R. 7, and any motion against a pro se litigant must comply with Civil L. R. 56(a).

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Settlement and ADR (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Settlement and ADR (trap): The court will refer the case to a magistrate judge for free mediation if asked at least 90 days before the final pretrial conference. Settlement discussions must be finished before the final pretrial conference. If a case settles after it, the court may impose jury-related costs (notification, travel, and attendance fees) on the responsible attorneys.

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Final pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Final pretrial and trial: Trial is set either at the scheduling conference or at the final pretrial conference; if the latter, the court aims for trial within 60–90 days. Motions in limine are due 14 days before the final pretrial conference and responses 7 days before. Under the standard form order, attorneys for all parties must appear in person at the final pretrial; parties need not appear but should be available by phone.

docs.t: Judge Brett H. Ludwig (E.D. Wis.) — Courtroom conduct
docs.x: Judge Brett H. Ludwig, E.D. Wis.. Courtroom conduct: Address clients, witnesses, and parties by surname, address arguments to the court rather than each other, and have only one attorney speak for a client on any issue unless permitted. Silence phones. The court has presentation equipment; coordinate with chambers staff (414-297-3071) to use other equipment or set up.

docs.t: Judge Byron B. Conway (E.D. Wis.) — Requests by motion only (trap)
docs.x: Judge Byron B. Conway, E.D. Wis.. Requests by motion only (trap): Never ask for court action by letter or stipulation; a request for an order must be made by motion (Fed. R. Civ. P. 7(b)(1)). Docket agreed requests as a “Stipulated Motion,” “Unopposed Motion,” or “Joint Motion”; incorrect docketing may mean the court does not act. Requests to reschedule any hearing or conference must be by motion, preferably joint. The court does not issue orders on stipulations of dismissal unless court approval is required by law; if it is, file a motion.

docs.t: Judge Byron B. Conway (E.D. Wis.) — Extensions and amendments
docs.x: Judge Byron B. Conway, E.D. Wis.. Extensions and amendments: Before seeking an extension, contact all parties where reasonable and say in the motion whether it is unopposed. Don’t wait until the deadline, and file extension motions as expedited motions under Civil Local Rule 7(h). Before moving to amend a pleading, ask the opponent to consent in writing so a motion may be unnecessary.

docs.t: Judge Byron B. Conway (E.D. Wis.) — Alert chambers to urgent filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Byron B. Conway, E.D. Wis.. Alert chambers to urgent filings (trap): The court gets no real-time filing notices, only a morning email of the previous day’s activity. Call chambers (920-301-4314) about any filing needing immediate attention, including anything filed the same day as a hearing. When you settle, notify the court as soon as possible, especially if a motion is pending or trial is set.

docs.t: Judge Byron B. Conway (E.D. Wis.) — Briefing format and page limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Byron B. Conway, E.D. Wis.. Briefing format and page limits (trap): Comply with the page limits in Civil L.R. 7(f), 7(h)(2), 16(c)(A), and 56(b)(8)(A) and the format rules of General L.R. 5(a). Do not evade limits with smaller margins, less than double spacing, or smaller fonts. Use footnotes sparingly if at all; put citations in the text, and never use footnotes for substantive arguments or to preserve arguments. Most motions are decided on the briefs; a request for oral argument must give specific reasons. No courtesy copies unless the court asks.

docs.t: Judge Byron B. Conway (E.D. Wis.) — Filing and the record
docs.x: Judge Byron B. Conway, E.D. Wis.. Filing and the record: Filings must be text-searchable. Give exhibits descriptive docket titles (for example, “Exhibit A – Smith Declaration,” not just “Exhibit A”). Where practical, cite documents already on the docket by ECF number (for example, “Smith Dec., ECF No. 123”), and don’t refile a document already in the record; cite the copy already filed.

docs.t: Judge Byron B. Conway (E.D. Wis.) — Sealing and restricting
docs.x: Judge Byron B. Conway, E.D. Wis.. Sealing and restricting: Every request to seal or restrict must fully comply with Gen. L.R. 79(d) and be supported by good cause; a party’s confidentiality designation alone is not enough. Generally file a redacted public version plus a restricted or sealed unredacted version. If the confidential material is irrelevant, file only a redacted version; file no public version only when redaction is impractical.

docs.t: Judge Byron B. Conway (E.D. Wis.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Byron B. Conway, E.D. Wis.. Discovery disputes (trap): Meet and confer in good faith before filing on every discovery dispute (Civ. L.R. 37). An email exchange noting outstanding discovery is not enough; communications must make clear that a motion is imminent and identify specifically what the movant will seek.

docs.t: Judge Byron B. Conway (E.D. Wis.) — Proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Byron B. Conway, E.D. Wis.. Proposed orders: Email proposed orders to ConwayPO@wied.uscourts.gov (for nothing else). Submit them for protective orders (which must state all terms rather than incorporate another document), class or collective action settlements, stipulated remands of Social Security cases, procedural and settlement-related orders in qui tam cases, and whenever one would help.

docs.t: Judge Lynn Adelman (E.D. Wis.) — Proposed orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge Lynn Adelman, E.D. Wis.. Proposed orders (trap): E-file every proposed order on the docket and also email an editable Word copy to AdelmanPO@wied.uscourts.gov. Without the Word copy, processing may be delayed or the court may ask for it before entering an order. The mailbox is for proposed orders only; no ex parte communications unless they relate to a proposed order or a pre-mediation statement.

docs.t: Judge Lynn Adelman (E.D. Wis.) — Requests to the court
docs.x: Judge Lynn Adelman, E.D. Wis.. Requests to the court: Requests for review or action, including hearing scheduling, must be filed in the case; requests made by other means, such as phone, may not be honored. Direct filing-procedure questions to the Clerk’s Office (414-297-3372).

docs.t: Judge Lynn Adelman (E.D. Wis.) — Paper copies
docs.x: Judge Lynn Adelman, E.D. Wis.. Paper copies: The judge’s former standing order requiring paper copies of all e-filed documents has not been in effect since April 6, 2022.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Motions, not letters (trap)
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Motions, not letters (trap): If you want the court to do something, file a motion; to just provide information, file a “notice.” Don’t write letters. Stipulations: file a signed “Stipulation,” then a one- or two-sentence motion asking the court to approve it and enter an order (proposed order attached), and email the proposed order in Word to PepperPO@wied.uscourts.gov, listing everything the court should order, with a signature block. Extension and adjournment motions should state how much time is needed and be filed before the day of the deadline or hearing. Filing by fax is permitted only rarely, with the judge’s permission.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Chambers contact and urgent filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Chambers contact and urgent filings (trap): Call the chambers group line (414-297-3335), not staff direct lines. Staff can’t give legal advice; the judicial assistant and courtroom deputy handle scheduling. Chambers gets no filing notices, only a daily activity report of the previous day’s filings, so a filing may go unseen for 24 hours or more. Call chambers if the judge needs to know about a filing right away; a Civil L.R. 7(h) expedited motion won’t necessarily get immediate attention without a call explaining the urgency. If the building closes for weather, call anyway; each judge decides whether to cancel hearings.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Proposed orders and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Proposed orders and courtesy copies: Proposed orders go on the docket as an attachment to the motion and also in Word (not PDF) to PepperPO@wied.uscourts.gov, so the judge can edit them. That mailbox is only for proposed orders, not correspondence. No paper courtesy copies.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Hearings and phone appearances
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Hearings and phone appearances: The judge decides whether a motion needs a hearing. To reschedule, file a joint motion or call the group line with all parties on; if not all agree, the requesting party must move (perhaps under Civil L.R. 7(h)). Many hearings are by phone (551-285-1373, Meeting ID 161 4901 8989, Passcode 190021); calling in on time is the parties’ responsibility. Any party may still appear in person. No evidence is taken by phone; hearings with testimony are set in person. Hearings are electronically recorded; ask by motion or at a hearing if you need a court reporter.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Civil cases
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Civil cases: The court sets a scheduling conference and requires a joint Rule 26(f) plan a couple of weeks before; it may cancel the conference after reviewing the plan. File discovery motions when legal issues need briefing, but only after good-faith efforts to resolve them. On a notice of settlement, the case is administratively closed; the parties must file the settlement papers and ask the court to convert the closure. Default judgment: the court first checks the record for proper service and may set a hearing if unclear. Attach proof, damages calculations, and fee and cost itemizations to avoid a prove-up hearing.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Injunctions and emergencies
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Injunctions and emergencies: For a truly urgent hearing, call chambers with the other party on the line and explain why and when. No “emergency” hearing is set unless you call and the other side has notice and can appear.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Criminal cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Criminal cases (trap): A change-of-plea hearing will not be scheduled until the signed plea agreement is filed on the docket. If the defendant’s presence is not required or is waived, consider requesting a phone hearing; defense counsel must inform the defendant and report back afterward. Hearings requiring the defendant’s presence are in person. The judge issues a criminal pretrial order once a case is referred with final pretrial and trial dates. The COVID-era video-hearing procedures still posted require a motion with three agreed alternative dates to move a hearing and a notice of non-consent for in-person hearings; they appear outdated.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Pretrial filings
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Pretrial filings: The pretrial order usually requires pretrial reports, exhibit and witness lists, voir dire questions, jury instructions, verdict forms, and motions in limine, due no later than 7 days before the final pretrial conference. If no order arrives within a couple of weeks of that conference, call chambers. By the final pretrial conference, email Word versions of voir dire questions, the full text of all proposed jury instructions (including pattern ones), and verdict forms to PepperPO@wied.uscourts.gov. Use Seventh Circuit pattern instructions where appropriate.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Jury selection: The judge asks voir dire questions, then hears follow-up requests at sidebar. In criminal trials the posted standard questions and process apply, so submit only additional questions or objections. For civil trials, don’t propose the standard background questions the judge always asks. Criminal: the government has 6 and the defense 10 peremptories (multiple defendants count as one party), exercised alternately from 28 venire members; each side then strikes one of the next four, leaving two alternates. Civil juries are 8 to 12 jurors.

docs.t: Judge Pamela Pepper (E.D. Wis.) — Trial and courtroom procedure (trap)
docs.x: Judge Pamela Pepper, E.D. Wis.. Trial and courtroom procedure (trap): Trial days run 9 a.m. to between 5 and 5:30 p.m. Pre-mark exhibits (no stickers are kept in the courtroom), agree on a numbering scheme, use one number for shared exhibits, and give the court a thumb drive (not a CD) of all exhibits. Admitted exhibits can’t be changed without approval. State objections in a word or two; argument happens at sidebar. Address the judge, not opposing counsel. Lawyers may not enter the jury box. Contact the courtroom deputy well before (more than a day) to test courtroom technology. Jurors may take notes only if all parties agree. Instruction conferences come before closings. General L.R. 47(c) is enforced: no contact with venire members or jurors, including alternates, before, during, or after trial without leave. Don’t post about the trial on social media, and tell clients and witnesses n

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Streamlined summary judgment option (trap)
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Streamlined summary judgment option (trap): Besides ordinary Civil L.R. 56 motions (stipulated facts under Civil L.R. 56(b)(5) are encouraged), a party may use the judge’s Streamlined Summary Judgment (SSJ) Procedure for a narrow, discrete issue resolvable early without extensive discovery, such as limitations, statute of frauds, contract interpretation, or conclusive video evidence. On request, the court may stay unrelated discovery or extend response time for related discovery. SSJ motions need no proposed findings of fact or responses; each side is limited to three affidavits of no more than five pages each (excluding exhibits) absent leave. Civil L.R. 56 page limits and deadlines otherwise apply. The motion must clearly say it uses the SSJ Procedure. Against a pro se party, comply with Civil L.R. 56(a) but omit the text of Civil L.R. 56. A later

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Extensions and agreed relief
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Extensions and agreed relief: Before seeking an extension, leave to amend, an enlarged brief, or similar relief, confer with all parties where reasonable and state whether the motion is opposed. Any extension request, including a stipulation, must give reasons so the court can find good cause under Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(b).

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Emergencies and expedited motions
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Emergencies and expedited motions: For immediate or emergency relief, call the deputy clerk or chambers directly; unless ex parte relief is warranted, the court generally sets a telephone status conference once opposing counsel is notified. Non-dispositive matters needing expedited attention use Civil L.R. 7(h); the court will call if a phone conference is needed.

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Discovery disputes: Confer before filing any discovery motion (Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(a), Civil L.R. 37). If available, the court will promptly hold a phone conference on disputes arising at or before a deposition. Complex disputes generally go by written motion, but the parties may ask for a phone conference before filing if the Rule 37 conference fails; such requests are frequently granted.

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Motions practice
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Motions practice: Raise objections to another party’s submission in your merits brief, not a separate motion to strike. Most motions are decided on the briefs; tell the court if you want argument and why. Email proposed orders in Word (not PDF) to GriesbachPO@wied.uscourts.gov, with the case number and relief in the subject line (e.g., “08-C-999 Order Extending Time”). None needed for summary judgment, contested motions to dismiss, or similar motions likely to get a written decision.

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Exhibits in e-filing
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Exhibits in e-filing: File exhibits as separately named attachments, or for many exhibits, as a combined PDF bookmarked to each exhibit and named to show the range (e.g., “Exhibits 1-25 bookmarked”); split into several files if the size limit requires. For sealed or restricted exhibits, put a redacted version or placeholder in the combined PDF and file each sealed exhibit as a separate, descriptively labeled attachment.

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Scheduling conference: After all parties appear, the court notices a Rule 16(b) conference, with the due date for the Rule 26(f) discovery plan. Counsel who know the case should attend, ready to discuss claim value, discovery, defenses, threshold issues, and a schedule.

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Pretrial and trial: Civil motions in limine are generally due at least 14 days before the final pretrial conference, with responses 7 days later; earlier filing of complex ones is appreciated. Trial generally starts at 9 a.m. with counsel there at 8:30 a.m. (at least on day one) and adjourns about 5 p.m. Matters outside the jury’s presence should be raised at breaks, before trial starts, or after the jury leaves. The court conducts voir dire, incorporating counsel’s questions, and usually seats eight jurors in civil cases. Jurors may take notes; instructions are generally read before closings.

docs.t: Judge William C. Griesbach (E.D. Wis.) — Exhibits and courtroom conduct (trap)
docs.x: Judge William C. Griesbach, E.D. Wis.. Exhibits and courtroom conduct (trap): Pre-mark exhibits sequentially, one number per item for the whole trial: 1–999 for plaintiff or prosecution, 1000–1999 for defendant, and further blocks of 1000 for additional parties (ask the clerk). Don’t show exhibits to the jury before admission absent stipulation; stipulating to admission beforehand is encouraged. Address everyone by surname and speak to the court, not each other. State objection grounds briefly; sidebars are short, and a full record can be made after the jury leaves. An easel and projector screen are available; bring your own laptop or other technology and arrange setup time with staff. Video testimony is available in some cases, including prisoner cases. Hearings are digitally recorded.

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Motion bundling (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. Motion bundling (trap): Do not file a motion, response, or reply until the motion is fully briefed or the briefing deadline has passed. Serve each paper and file only a dated Certificate of Service (ECF event “Certificate of Service”), which counts as the filing date. Within one business day after full briefing, the parties file all papers in order (motion, response, reply) and the movant files a Notice of compliance stating the motion is fully briefed. An early-filed motion is terminated without prejudice; a compliant certificate filed within one business day relates back. Exceptions: remand motions, cases with a pro se party, Rule 55(b)(2) default judgment, Rule 50(b)/52(b)/59/60 motions, ex parte motions, motions to seal and for leave (filed immediately before the document), emergency motions under L.R. CV-7(l), and motions where waiting could impa

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Format and length (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. Format and length (trap): Number every page in the bottom margin starting with 1 on the first page, even a cover page; no Roman numerals (exhibits and independently prepared forms excepted). Every page counts toward page limits except pages bearing only a caption, tables, signature block, or certificates; incorporating a prior filing by reference counts its pages. Embed the table of contents and add PDF bookmarks where hard copy would have tabs. Bluebook citations, with italics instead of underscoring, and for unreported cases a Westlaw cite plus full docket number and date. Violations lead to striking or termination without prejudice. Motions to extend page limits are granted only in exceptional circumstances.

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Proposed orders and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. Proposed orders and courtesy copies: Each proposed order required by L.R. CV-7(a) must state the specific relief sought (not just “motion granted”), bear the case style and number, and be titled “[Proposed] Order”; otherwise the motion is terminated without prejudice. Injunction orders must meet Rule 65(d) detail. Judge Barker has not opted out of L.R. CV-5(a)(9) courtesy copies; double-sided printing and spiral binding for larger documents are encouraged.

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. Sealing (trap): A motion to seal must cite authority on sealing judicial records, not just L.R. CV-5(a)(7) or a protective order (June Medical v. Phillips), and explain why redaction won’t do if sealing a whole document. For redaction-only sealing, justify each redaction and, by the deadline for publicly filing the redacted version, email a highlighted unredacted copy to Chambers_of_Judge_Barker@txed.uscourts.gov. The court may return marked redactions to remove, to be refiled within 7 days. Noncompliance means denial and striking of the sealed document; a refiled document does not relate back. No proposed order is needed; Form JCB-CV-5.1 on the page lists the grounds for denial and works as a checklist.

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. Discovery: Before moving to compel, quash, or for protection, lead counsel must confer in good faith and consider the discovery hotline, (903) 590-1198; the motion must certify those steps, including whether the hotline was called or why not. Emergency or expedited discovery motions won’t be heard unless each movant first used the hotline and then promptly moved regarding the magistrate judge’s ruling. Parties with extensive e-discovery disputes must review the model e-discovery order first: no metadata or email in general requests, email requests limited to 8 custodians and 10 search terms per custodian per producing party, and no backup restoration absent good cause.

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Early deadlines and class actions (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. Early deadlines and class actions (trap): Plaintiff must file a notice of readiness for a scheduling conference within 5 days after all non-stayed defendants have answered or otherwise responded. In a putative class action, plaintiff must move for class certification within 90 days after filing, unless extended.

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Scheduling order template
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. Scheduling order template: Notice of mediator 21 days after the scheduling order (court appoints one if no agreement); joinder and amendment motions at 61 days; burden-of-proof experts at 117 days and opposing experts at 145 days; rebuttal experts within 30 days; mediation by 175 days, with a joint report within 7 days. Discovery closes about 205 days before trial; parties may extend it by joint notice only if no other date is affected. Requests to move trial must be made in writing before the discovery deadline. Agreements of counsel to extend deadlines do not bind the court. The mandatory-disclosure version adds a court-set deadline to disclose witnesses with summaries, L.R. CV-34 records, and all relevant documents; the bench-trial version drops the jury charge and voir dire items.

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Settlement
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. Settlement: By 28 days before trial, parties and lead counsel must hold a face-to-face settlement meeting with representatives with settlement authority and any liability insurer with authority to offer policy limits, all in person; file a joint report within 7 days. On settlement in principle, promptly file a “Notice of settlement and joint motion to stay all deadlines” affirming all matters have settled and requesting a stay for a stated period (good cause for over 30 days), or deadlines are not stayed. A Rule 41(a)(1) notice or stipulation dismisses without court action; no motion to dismiss is needed. Counsel must advise clients about mediation, arbitration, and other ADR.

Joint final pretrial report 45 days before trial (Word copy emailed to the same address), with a 1–3 page executive summary per party, an agreed jury questionnaire, joint instructions and verdict form, and each party’s certification that its lead trial attorney re-read all the Federal Rules of Evidence within the past 6 months. Motions in limine 45 days before trial, not filed as a matter of course, after meet-and-confer; responses 30 days; no replies without leave. Exchange marked exhibits and deliver a set to chambers 28 days before trial, and file time requests for voir

docs.t: Judge J. Campbell Barker (E.D. Tex.) — Criminal cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Campbell Barker, E.D. Tex.. docs.x: Judge Jeremy Kernodle, E.D. Tex.. Disclosure statements (trap): At its first appearance in any civil or miscellaneous case (including after removal), each party must file, as a standalone docket entry, a signed certificate of interested persons with the Rule 7.1(a) information plus every person or entity financially interested in the outcome (parents, affiliates, guarantors, insurers, and so on). A party may adopt another party’s certificate by reference if it agrees it is accurate. Supplement within 10 business days of any change.

docs.t: Judge Jeremy Kernodle (E.D. Tex.) — Magistrate judge referrals
docs.x: Judge Jeremy Kernodle, E.D. Tex.. Magistrate judge referrals: Referral Order JDK-72-2 (2019) withdrew the earlier order that referred 40% of Tyler civil cases to Magistrate Judges Love and Mitchell, without affecting cases already referred or special-category referrals. Motions to extend deadlines are not emergencies.

Supp., F.R.D., S.W., or Vernon’s Texas statutes must be attached in an appendix, together with any affidavits, deposition testimony, or discovery cited; appendices need a paginated table of contents. Submission dates may be extended by agreement before they expire, via a joint motion with an agreed order, unless a court deadline is affected. Motions to extend discovery or motion deadlines must be filed early enough for a res

docs.t: Judge Marcia A. Crone (E.D. Tex.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Marcia A. Crone, E.D. Tex.. Summary judgment (trap): Every dispositive motion brief must include the nature and stage of the case, a list of undisputed material facts in separately numbered sentences with record cites, the issues with the standard of review for each, argument under headings, and a conclusion stating the precise relief; briefs with more than 10 pages of argument also need tables of contents and authorities and a summary of argument. The response must answer each numbered fact with “undisputed,” “disputed” plus a record cite, or a short explanatory phrase. A non-movant needing more discovery must say exactly what, from whom, and by when, and may add numbered facts of its own. Only one summary judgment motion per party without leave.

docs.x: Judge Marcia A. Crone, E.D. Tex.. Sanctions can include fines, dismissal, and disciplinary referral.

No motion other than limine motions, including expert challenges, may be filed after the motion cut-off without good cause. If none is pending then, file a joint status report on trial readiness. docs.x: Judge Marcia A. Crone, E.D. Tex.. On the filing day, deliver two color-printed courtesy copies in three-ring notebooks with dividers. Failure to file or appear can mean dismissal. Authentication challenges must be made in writing within 3 business days, or authenticity is conceded. docs.t: Judge Marcia A. Crone (E.D. Tex.) — Trial settings and continuances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Marcia A. Crone, E.D. Tex.. Trial settings and continuances (trap): Civil cases are set for trial at the final status conference; pending motions and objections are ruled on at the final pretrial conference. Criminal final pretrial conferences are the second Monday of each month at 9 a.m., with trial starting immediately after. Joint continuance motions are not binding. Trials are not continued for an unavailable witness; use a deposition or stipulation. Prior settings don’t justify a continuance unless counsel has actually begun another trial. Vacation requests made well in advance are respected.

docs.t: Judge Marcia A. Crone (E.D. Tex.) — Trial and courtroom conduct
docs.x: Judge Marcia A. Crone, E.D. Tex.. Trial and courtroom conduct: Court usually sits 9 a.m. to about 6 p.m., with a 1 hour 15 minute lunch. In civil trials, counsel supply a notepad and pen for each juror on day one. Counsel set up their own equipment, with advance permission from the court administrator. Examine witnesses and give openings and closings from the lectern; stand when addressing the court; no permission needed to approach a witness unless the court asks. Business attire is required (detailed dress code in MC-83). Stay near the courtroom during deliberations. Courthouse security orders for Beaumont and Lufkin bar liquids (including water bottles), laser pointers, lighters, and vape pens without a judge’s approval.

docs.t: Judge Marcia A. Crone (E.D. Tex.) — Settlement and dismissal
docs.x: Judge Marcia A. Crone, E.D. Tex.. Settlement and dismissal: Parties must make good-faith settlement efforts early; the court may order mediation. Immediately notify the court administrator of a settlement in any case with pending motions or a setting; closing papers are due within 30 days of the announcement. Minor settlements: jointly move for a guardian ad litem when there is a potential conflict, request a settlement conference by letter, and furnish the proposed judgment beforehand; all counsel and parties must attend. Defendants not served within 120 days after filing will be dismissed without prejudice absent good cause (as stated in the 2005 order).

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Truncale (E.D. Tex.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Truncale, E.D. Tex.. Courtesy copies (trap): Judge Truncale has opted out of L.R. Follow the order entered in your case.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Truncale (E.D. Tex.) — Oral argument and newer attorneys
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Truncale, E.D. Tex.. Oral argument and newer attorneys: If a party wants an attorney practicing less than seven years to argue a ripe motion, contact chambers to request oral argument and say so. The court will grant argument if at all practicable, even where it would otherwise rule on the papers, may allow extra time, lets senior counsel also speak, and asks the other side to reciprocate. No inference is drawn from a party’s choice whether to use a newer attorney.

Before the 26(f) conference counsel must discuss settlement and magistrate-judge consent with clients. Absent agreement, no depositions before the Rule 16 conference. docs.x: Judge Michael J. Truncale, E.D. Tex.. Patent discovery limits: Per side: 40 interrogatories, 40 requests for admission, 70 hours of fact depositions, and 7 hours per expert report. docs.t: Judge R. Brooke Jackson (D. Colo.) — Page limits and briefing (trap)
docs.x: Judge R. Brooke Jackson, D. Colo.. Page limits and briefing (trap): Motions and responses 15 pages, replies 5; summary judgment motions and responses 20 pages, replies 10.
